summary: Describes how a DNS recursive resolver can run a copy of the root zone locally. This cuts round-trip times to root servers and prevents third parties from watching the queries sent to them.

eli5.summary: Rather than calling the head librarian every time, you keep your own copy of the index at home.

subtitle: How a DNS resolver can keep its own copy of the root zone, safely, and fall back when it goes stale.

tldr.problem: Some resolvers are far from the nearest root server and may struggle to get answers during an attack. Their queries to the root can also be observed by third parties.
tldr.mechanism: The resolver serves a full copy of the root zone from its own host, validates it with DNSSEC, answers only itself, and refreshes it using the SOA timers.
tldr.outcome: It cuts round-trip time and hides root queries, at the cost of some operational fragility. If the copy cannot be refreshed before it expires, the resolver MUST switch back to the normal root servers.

today: RFC 8806 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 7706, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its example configurations name software versions current at its publication in June 2020.

sections.title: Why Run the Root Locally
sections.content:
A recursive resolver must answer every client query, even for names that do not exist. For a top-level domain (TLD) not in its cache, it has to ask a root server. The RFC says research shows the vast majority of queries to the root are for names that do not exist in the root zone, and that many answers are referrals that third parties might observe on the network.

The primary goals are more reliable answers during attacks on the root servers and keeping queries and responses off the network. The RFC expects little speed-up for good queries, because TLD records usually have a long TTL (on the order of a day or two) and are already cached.

The design is not free: if the local system does not work correctly, users can get bad data or resolution can fail in ways that are hard to diagnose. RFC 7706 was controversial when published, but the RFC says the DNS operational community has largely come to see local serving of the root zone for an individual resolver as reasonable.
sections.eli5: If you keep a copy of the phone book at home, nobody can see whom you look up and you can still find numbers when the phone lines are busy. But you must keep your copy fresh.

sections.title: What the System Must Be Able to Do
sections.content:
To use this method the system MUST do all of the following:

  • Validate every signed record in a zone with DNSSEC.
  • Hold an up-to-date copy of the public part of the root Key Signing Key (KSK).
  • Retrieve the entire root zone, including all DNSSEC-related records.
  • Run an authoritative service for the root zone on the same host, answering only queries from that host.

Two ways to meet the last rule are an authoritative server listening only on a loopback address (127/8 for IPv4, or ::1 in IPv6), or resolver software that also acts as an authoritative server for the root, but only for itself.

The local data MUST be identical to the real root zone. Glue records could be changed, but that could cause problems, so changes to glue SHOULD NOT be made.
sections.eli5: Your copy has to be an exact photocopy, it has to carry the official stamp so you can check it is real, and only you may read it.

sections.title: Setting Up and Refreshing the Copy
sections.content:
There are two steps: retrieve a copy of the root zone, then start an authoritative service for it in a way that stops any system other than a recursive resolver on the same host from reaching it. The service can run separately from the resolver or be part of its configuration.

The zone MUST be refreshed using the timers in the root zone's SOA record, as described in RFC 1035. The local copy will therefore likely lag a little behind the global servers, which update on NOTIFY messages.

If the copy cannot be refreshed before the SOA expire time, the system MUST NOT serve stale data and MUST immediately switch to non-local root servers. The RFC warns the results of failed refreshing can be disastrous, for example when all the NS records for a TLD change within a short period such as 2 days.

Administrators SHOULD have an automated check that the copy is being refreshed. One way is a separate process that watches the SOA serial. When the RFC was published the root SOA was the current date with a two-digit counter appended and changed every day, for example 2019010201 for January 2, 2019.
sections.eli5: Check your copy of the index often. If it is too old to trust, stop using it right away and phone the library again.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7706
sections.content:
RFC 7706 required a root server instance on the loopback interface of the host running the validating resolver. RFC 8806 loosens that: any local service is allowed, not necessarily an authoritative server, as long as only systems on that single host can query it.

It also removes the prohibition on distributing recursive DNS servers with this configuration, adds the idea of switching to the normal remote root servers if the local one fails, refreshes the list of places to get the root zone, and adds and updates example configurations.
sections.eli5: The old rule said the copy had to live in one exact drawer. The new rule says any place in your own house is fine, as long as nobody outside can reach it.

sections.title: Sources of the Root Zone and Example Configurations
sections.content:
Appendix A says the root zone can come from anywhere if it includes all the DNSSEC records needed for validation. At publication, it could be fetched by AXFR over TCP from ICANN servers (xfr.lax.dns.icann.org and xfr.cjr.dns.icann.org) and from the b, c, d, f, g and k root server operators. None of these are guaranteed to stay available. LocalRoot is described as an experimental service that embodies many of the ideas in the document.

Appendix B gives example fragments for BIND 9.12 and 9.14, Unbound 1.8 and 1.9, Knot Resolver and Microsoft Windows Server 2012, described as software believed to implement the requirements correctly. For example, BIND 9.14 can mirror the root zone with type mirror, because a default list of primary servers for the IANA root zone is built in.
sections.eli5: You can get a copy of the index from several official places, and the appendix shows how to ask a few popular programs to do the copying for you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A system that skips the DNSSEC requirements can be fooled into giving bad responses, in the same way as any resolver that does not validate answers from a remote root server. Anyone deploying this should understand the benefits and costs of DNSSEC.

The local copy must be available only to resolvers on the same host. That limits the damage to clients of any local resolver that might rely on an altered copy of the root.
sections.eli5: Always check the official stamp on your copy, and never hand your copy to other people, so a bad copy can only hurt you.
